definition: To look steadily at something for a long time
example: We sat on the hill to gaze at the stars.
origin: From Middle English gasen “to stare”, probably of Scandinavian origin; compare Swedish dialect gasa “to gape”.
quote: I saw his dark face lit up with a boyish enthusiasm as he gazed about him.
quote_source: Arthur Conan Doyle, The Hound of the Baskervilles

definition: To feel deep sadness, especially after a death
example: The whole town continued to grieve for the lost fishermen.
origin: From Old French grever “to burden, to afflict”, from Latin gravare “to make heavy”, from gravis “heavy”.
quote: If you had murdered our father, it would grieve me that you should reject your punishment.

definition: To stay somewhere longer than necessary
example: Guests tend to linger in the garden long after dinner is over.
origin: From Middle English lengeren “to dwell”, a frequentative of lengen “to prolong”, from Old English lengan, related to long.
quote: The dragons have gone, and so have the knights, but still she lingers in our midst.
quote_source: E. M. Forster, A Room with a View

definition: To dislike someone or something intensely
example: I loathe waiting in line at the airport.
origin: From Old English lathian “to be hateful”, from lath “hostile, hateful”.
quote: The more she gave up herself to the one, the more she loathed the other.

definition: To repair something broken or damaged
example: My grandfather taught me how to mend a torn fishing net.
origin: Shortened from amend, from Old French amender, from Latin emendare “to free from fault”, from menda “fault”.
quote: Whether from lack of time or from indifference, she no longer mended her linen.

definition: To ask for something in an urgent, emotional way
example: The prisoners plead for mercy, but the judge is unmoved.
origin: From Old French plaidier “to go to law”, from plait “lawsuit”, from Latin placitum “decree, opinion”, literally “what is pleasing”.
quote: At first she wouldn’t come at all; and then she pleaded for five minutes by my watch.

definition: To follow or chase in order to catch or achieve
example: She moved to Vienna to pursue a career in music.
origin: From Anglo-French pursuer, from Latin prosequi “to follow after”, from pro- “forward” and sequi “to follow”.
quote: One thought, and one only, pursued her in different forms, and refused to be shaken off.

definition: To feel or show great joy
example: Fans rejoice whenever the team wins at home.
origin: From Old French rejoiss-, stem of rejoir “to gladden”, from re- (intensive) and joir “to be glad”, from Latin gaudere “to be glad”.
quote: With all my soul I wish them happy, and rejoice over every circumstance in favour of it.

definition: To speak angrily to someone who has done wrong
example: Parents should not scold a child for asking honest questions.
origin: From Middle English scold “a quarrelsome, abusive person”, probably from Old Norse skáld “poet”, as a writer of mocking verse.
quote: You have scolded me too much for match-making, for me to presume to take such a liberty with you.

definition: To take hold of something suddenly and firmly
example: Police were able to seize the stolen paintings at the border.
origin: From Old French seisir “to take possession of”, from medieval Latin sacire, probably of Germanic origin.
quote: I seized the opportunity of slightly shifting my position, which had become cramped, and then listened.
quote_source: H. G. Wells, The War of the Worlds

definition: To surprise or frighten someone suddenly
example: A loud knock on the window will startle the sleeping dog.
origin: From Old English steartlian “to kick, to struggle”, related to start in its old sense “to leap”.
quote: Here perhaps in some southern wood an old man lit dry ferns and the birds were startled.

definition: To walk around slowly with no clear direction
example: We love to wander through the old streets of Lisbon at night.
origin: From Old English wandrian “to move about aimlessly”, related to wend and wind.
quote: Raskolnikov particularly liked this place and the neighbouring alleys, when he wandered aimlessly in the streets.

definition: To die, especially in a sudden or violent way
example: Without water, the young plants will perish within days.
origin: From Old French periss-, stem of perir, from Latin perire “to pass away, to be lost”, from per- “through, away” and ire “to go”.
quote: One can perish from being undermined as well as from being struck by lightning.

definition: To say something in a soft, quiet voice
example: I heard him murmur an apology as he left the room.
origin: From Old French murmurer, from Latin murmurare, from murmur “a hum, a muttering”, an imitative word.
quote: The murmur trembled on the verge of coherence, sank down, mounted excitedly, and then ceased altogether.
quote_source: F. Scott Fitzgerald, The Great Gatsby

definition: A careless or stupid mistake
example: Sending the email to the whole company was an embarrassing blunder.
origin: From Middle English blunderen “to stumble about blindly”, probably of Scandinavian origin; compare Old Norse blunda “to shut the eyes”.
quote: In another plate, the prodigious blunder is made of representing the whale with perpendicular flukes.

definition: The darker part of twilight, just before night
example: Bats leave the cave at dusk to hunt for insects.
origin: From Middle English dosk “dark, dim”, from Old English dox “dark, swarthy”.
quote: When the short days of winter came dusk fell before we had well eaten our dinners.

definition: An achievement that needs great skill or courage
example: Crossing the ocean alone in a rowing boat was an extraordinary feat.
origin: From Anglo-French fet, Old French fait, from Latin factum “a thing done”, from facere “to do”.
quote: Do you think that you could perform one more feat?
quote_source: Arthur Conan Doyle, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes

definition: A lack of good sense; a foolish act
example: It would be folly to sail in such a violent storm.
origin: From Old French folie “madness”, from fol “foolish, mad”, from Latin follis “bellows, bag of wind”.
quote: Not a single sprouting ambition committed the folly of putting forth its foliage in his shadow.

definition: Partial darkness, or a feeling of sadness
example: A single candle did little to lift the gloom of the hall.
origin: Related to Old English glom “twilight”; in Middle English the verb gloumen meant “to frown, to look sullen”.
quote: No golden light had ever been so precious as the gloom of this dark forest.

definition: A lasting feeling of anger about a past wrong
example: He has held a grudge against his brother for twenty years.
origin: From Middle English grucchen “to murmur, to complain”, from Old French grouchier “to grumble”, of uncertain origin.
quote: I bear you no grudge; I think no worse of you than I do of other people.

definition: Playful behavior that causes minor trouble
example: The twins were always getting into mischief when left alone.
origin: From Old French meschief “misfortune”, from meschever “to come to grief”, from mes- “badly” and chever “to come to an end”, from chief “head, end”.
quote: There was a gleam of mischief in her big dark eyes with their long lashes.

definition: Deep regret for something you did wrong
example: The driver showed no remorse for the accident he caused.
origin: From Old French remors, from medieval Latin remorsus, from Latin remordere “to bite again, to torment”, from mordere “to bite”.
quote: Levin immediately felt the reproach in the eyes fixed on him, and felt remorse at his own happiness.

definition: The state of being alone, often by choice
example: After a noisy week she enjoyed the solitude of the mountains.
origin: From Old French solitude, from Latin solitudo “loneliness”, from solus “alone”.
quote: In solitude a man generally listens to the first voice, but in society to the second.

definition: A feeling of deep sadness or loss
example: Words cannot express our sorrow at the news of his death.
origin: From Old English sorg “grief, care, anxiety”.
quote: Oh! how easy for those, who have no sorrow of their own to talk of exertion!

definition: Long, hard and tiring work
example: After years of toil, the farm finally began to make money.
origin: From Anglo-French toiller “to agitate, to stir up, to entangle”; the sense “hard work” grew out of “struggle, turmoil”.
quote: All the long day of toil had left no trace in them but lightness of heart.

definition: A sudden wish or idea, often an odd one
example: On a whim, we booked two tickets to Iceland that same evening.
origin: Shortened from whim-wham “a fanciful object, a trinket”, of unknown origin.
quote: Follies and nonsense, whims and inconsistencies, do divert me, I own, and I laugh at them whenever I can.

definition: A wish to have what another person has
example: Her new car was the envy of the whole neighborhood.
origin: From Old French envie, from Latin invidia, from invidere “to look at with ill will”, from in- “upon” and videre “to see”.
quote: Tom was a glittering hero once more—the pet of the old, the envy of the young.
quote_source: Mark Twain, The Adventures of Tom Sawyer

definition: More than enough in size or amount
example: There is ample room in the trunk for all four suitcases.
origin: From Old French ample, from Latin amplus “large, spacious, abundant”.
quote: All of us had an ample share of the treasure and used it wisely or foolishly, according to our natures.

definition: Lacking ease or grace; uncomfortable or embarrassing
example: There was an awkward silence after he forgot her name.
origin: From Middle English awk “turned the wrong way” (from Old Norse afugr) and -ward “in the direction of”.
quote: At such a time much might have been said, and silence was very awkward.

definition: Clever at getting what you want by tricks
example: The cunning fox waited until the farmer had gone inside.
origin: From Middle English cunning “knowing, skilled”, from cunnen “to know”, from Old English cunnan; related to can.
quote: The more cunning a man is, the simpler the trap he must be caught in.

definition: Dull, dark and making you feel sad
example: We spent a dreary afternoon waiting for the rain to stop.
origin: From Old English dreorig “sad, sorrowful”, originally “bloody, gory”, from dreor “gore, falling blood”.
quote: I wondered why moralists call this world a dreary wilderness: for me it blossomed like a rose.

definition: Violent and aggressive, or very strong
example: The two companies are locked in fierce competition for customers.
origin: From Old French fers, nominative of fer “wild, proud”, from Latin ferus “wild, untamed”.
quote: He’s not a rough diamond—a pearl-containing oyster of a rustic: he’s a fierce, pitiless, wolfish man.

definition: Very serious, gloomy or worrying
example: The doctor's grim expression told us the news was bad.
origin: From Old English grimm “fierce, savage, cruel”.
quote: There was a look of grim satisfaction in his face, as of one who has had a doubt solved.

definition: Very eager, or sharp and quick
example: She has a keen eye for detail and a keen interest in art.
origin: From Old English cene “bold, brave”, later “sharp”.
quote: There is so keen a sympathy between us that I should know if evil came upon him.
quote_source: Arthur Conan Doyle, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes

definition: Quick and light in movement or thought
example: A nimble goalkeeper can change direction in an instant.
origin: From Old English næmel “quick to grasp”, from niman “to take”; the b crept in later.
quote: She was a nimble little needlewoman, and they were finished before anyone got tired of them.

definition: Shining brightly, or glowing with joy
example: The bride looked radiant as she walked into the room.
origin: From Latin radians “shining”, from radiare “to emit rays”, from radius “ray, spoke”.
quote: Her flushed face, fringed with soft curling hair under her night cap, was radiant with joy and courage.

definition: Having sharp practical judgment
example: A shrewd investor, she sold her shares just before prices fell.
origin: From Middle English shrewed “wicked, cursed”, from shrew “a spiteful person”; the sense softened to “cunning” and then “clever”.
quote: He was a strong-minded man, sir, shrewd, practical, and as unimaginative as I am myself.
quote_source: Arthur Conan Doyle, The Hound of the Baskervilles

definition: Very serious, formal and dignified
example: The soldiers made a solemn promise to defend the city.
origin: From Old French solemne, from Latin sollemnis “established, ceremonial, performed at fixed times”.
quote: All manner of solemn nonsense was talked on the subject, but I believed none of it.

definition: Lacking courage or confidence; easily frightened
example: The timid boy stood at the back and never raised his hand.
origin: From Latin timidus “fearful”, from timere “to fear”.
quote: The gardener made a timid bow, and remained at the door of the cell.

definition: Extremely large in size, amount or extent
example: A vast desert stretches from the mountains to the sea.
origin: From Latin vastus “immense, empty, desolate”.
quote: Don’t I feel in my soul that I am part of this vast harmonious whole?

definition: Very unhappy, unfortunate or of poor quality
example: The refugees spent a wretched winter in thin canvas tents.
origin: From Middle English wrecched, from wrecche “wretch”, from Old English wrecca “exile, outcast”.
quote: Though the day was just as fine as yesterday, it seemed a wretched little place this time.

definition: Serious and sincere in what you say or do
example: He made an earnest attempt to repair the friendship.
origin: From Old English eornoste “serious, zealous”, from eornost “seriousness”.
quote: We shook hands, and he was so earnest and so kind that it made me quite choky.

definition: Easily broken, damaged or harmed
example: Pack the fragile glasses carefully between layers of newspaper.
origin: From Latin fragilis “easily broken”, from frangere “to break”.
quote: Despair is surrounded with fragile partitions which all open on either vice or crime.

definition: To regard with disgust and hatred
example: Most people abhor cruelty to animals in any form.
origin: From Latin abhorrere “to shrink back from in horror”, from ab- “away from” and horrere “to bristle, to shudder”.
quote: You, my creator, abhor me; what hope can I gather from your fellow creatures, who owe me nothing?

definition: To warn or criticize someone firmly but gently
example: The coach had to admonish two players for arriving late.
origin: From Old French amonester, from Latin admonere “to remind, to warn”, from ad- “to” and monere “to warn”.
quote: “You’re letting your supper get cold,” she admonished him with a pale gleam of gaiety.

definition: To mention something in an indirect way
example: She likes to allude to her years in Paris without giving details.
origin: From Latin alludere “to play with, to jest”, from ad- “to” and ludere “to play”.
quote: Besides, it struck him as a little absurd to allude to the matter.
quote_source: Edith Wharton, The Age of Innocence

definition: To calm someone by giving what they demand
example: The manager offered a refund to appease the angry customer.
origin: From Old French apaisier “to bring to peace”, from a- “to” and pais “peace”, from Latin pax.
quote: Hunger he had known; and when he could not appease his hunger he had felt restriction.

definition: To charm someone, sometimes in order to deceive
example: The salesman tried to beguile us with stories of easy profits.
origin: From be- “thoroughly” and guile “deceit”, from Old French guile, of Germanic origin.
quote: Finding that the social spirit had beguiled her into being rather late, she dressed hastily and went over to the parsonage rather earlier than was necessary.

definition: To ask for something in an anxious, urgent way
example: I beseech you to think again before you sign that contract.
origin: From Middle English besechen, from be- (intensive) and sechen “to seek”, from Old English secan.
quote: Don’t follow me, I beseech you, I have somewhere else to go....

definition: To think about something deeply and at length
example: He sat by the lake to contemplate his future.
origin: From Latin contemplari “to gaze at, to observe”, from con- (intensive) and templum, a space marked out for watching omens.
quote: I contemplate at least a temporary withdrawal from the management of much business, whether benevolent or commercial.

definition: The feeling that something deserves no respect
example: She looked at the cheap souvenirs with obvious disdain.
origin: From Old French desdeign, from desdeignier “to scorn”, from Latin dedignari “to reject as unworthy”, from de- “away” and dignari “to deem worthy”.
quote: The face was saturnine and swarthy, and the sensual lips seemed to be twisted with disdain.
quote_source: Oscar Wilde, The Picture of Dorian Gray

definition: To ask someone earnestly or anxiously
example: Let me entreat you once more to stay until morning.
origin: From Old French entraiter “to treat, to deal with”, from en- and traiter “to treat”, from Latin tractare “to handle”.
quote: I entreat you to hear me before you give vent to your hatred on my devoted head.

definition: To praise highly or raise in rank
example: The poem seems to exalt the simple life of the countryside.
origin: From Latin exaltare “to raise high”, from ex- “out, upward” and altus “high”.
quote: And, true enough, in proportion as he appeared to humble himself was he exalted.

definition: To beg someone desperately to do something
example: Doctors implore the public to stay home during the storm.
origin: From Latin implorare “to call upon with tears”, from in- “upon” and plorare “to weep, to cry out”.
quote: I implored the colonel to let me out, but the remorseless clanking of the levers drowned my cries.
quote_source: Arthur Conan Doyle, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes

definition: To grow weak or remain neglected for a long time
example: Thousands of applications languish in a queue for months.
origin: From Old French languiss-, stem of languir, from Latin languere “to be faint, to be weak”.
quote: The conversation languished; Madame Bovary gave it up every few minutes, whilst he himself seemed quite embarrassed.

definition: To confuse and worry someone
example: The strange results perplex the scientists who ran the experiment.
origin: From the older adjective perplex “confused”, from Latin perplexus “entangled”, from per- “thoroughly” and plectere “to weave, to braid”.
quote: What was there to frighten or to perplex in the prospect of life?

definition: To criticize someone sharply for what they did
example: The judge did not hesitate to rebuke the lawyer for his rudeness.
origin: From Anglo-French rebuker “to beat back”, from re- “back” and Old French buschier “to strike, to chop wood”, from busche “log”.
quote: Archer, changing colour, stood up also: it was the bitterest rebuke she could have given him.
quote_source: Edith Wharton, The Age of Innocence

definition: Blame or criticism for a fault or failure
example: His mother's eyes were full of silent reproach.
origin: From Old French reproche, from reprochier “to blame”, probably from Latin re- “back” and prope “near”: to bring something back close to someone.
quote: The man folded his arms and stared at the grating with an air of reproach.

definition: To refuse to accept or be connected with
example: The senator was quick to repudiate the remarks of his own adviser.
origin: From Latin repudiare “to divorce, to reject”, from repudium “divorce, rejection”.
quote: The charge of robbery I repudiate with indignation.

definition: To suppose something is true without firm proof
example: From the empty driveway I surmise that they have already left.
origin: From Old French surmis, past participle of surmettre “to accuse”, from sur- “upon” and mettre “to put”.
quote: Harriet had not surmised her own danger, but the idea of it struck her forcibly.

definition: To annoy, worry or frustrate someone
example: Small delays vex him far more than real disasters ever do.
origin: From Old French vexer, from Latin vexare “to shake, to harass, to trouble”.
quote: At the same time, he was horribly vexed because there was dust on his boots.

definition: To be unsteady or unable to decide
example: Her support for the plan began to waver after the first setback.
origin: From Middle English waveren, probably from Old Norse vafra “to flicker, to move unsteadily”.
quote: I wavered again, and began to think here were greater expectations than my own.

definition: Great enthusiasm or passion
example: They defended their small theater with surprising ardor.
origin: From Old French ardour, from Latin ardor “heat, flame”, from ardere “to burn”.
quote: The very nearness of the fire but cooled our ardor.

definition: Extreme greed for money or possessions
example: His avarice cost him every friend he ever had.
origin: From Old French avarice, from Latin avaritia, from avarus “greedy”, from avere “to crave”.
quote: They were influenced by hatred, by avarice, and by self-love; but I was base, and for want of courage acted against my judgment.
quote_source: Alexandre Dumas, The Count of Monte Cristo

definition: A sudden, unpredictable change of mood or behavior
example: The schedule seemed to change at the caprice of the director.
origin: From French caprice, from Italian capriccio “a sudden start, a shiver”, perhaps from capo “head” and riccio “hedgehog”: a head with the hair standing on end.
quote: Without conscious intention he began to clutch at every passing caprice, taking it for a desire and an object.

definition: The state of being calm and in control
example: She kept her composure even when the audience began to shout.
origin: From compose and the suffix -ure; compose comes from Old French composer “to put together”, from com- “together” and poser “to place”.
quote: Estella looked at her with perfect composure, and again looked down at the fire.

definition: Courage shown through pain or long difficulty
example: She bore the long illness with remarkable fortitude.
origin: From Latin fortitudo “strength”, from fortis “strong”.
quote: But active love is labor and fortitude, and for some people too, perhaps, a complete science.

definition: Anger at something that seems unfair or wrong
example: The decision to close the school caused widespread indignation.
origin: From Latin indignatio, from indignari “to regard as unworthy”, from in- “not” and dignus “worthy”.
quote: However just her indignation might be, her ideal was not to claim justice, but to give tenderness.

definition: A deep, lasting and thoughtful sadness
example: A gentle melancholy settled over him as the summer ended.
origin: From Greek melankholia, from melas “black” and khole “bile”; an excess of black bile was once thought to cause sadness.
quote: You are in a melancholy humour, and fancy that any one unlike yourself must be happy.

definition: A state of pleasant, dreamy thought
example: The ringing phone pulled her out of her reverie.
origin: From French rêverie, from rêver “to dream”, in Old French “to wander, to be delirious”, of uncertain origin.
quote: Helen sighed as her reverie fled, and getting up, obeyed the monitor without reply as without delay.

definition: A moral doubt that makes you hesitate
example: He had no scruple about reading other people's letters.
origin: From Latin scrupulus “a small sharp stone”, hence a source of unease, from scrupus “rough stone”.
quote: Notions and scruples were like spilt needles, making one afraid of treading, or sitting down, or even eating.

definition: A loud, confused noise or state of disorder
example: The speaker could not be heard above the tumult of the crowd.
origin: From Latin tumultus “commotion, uproar”, related to tumere “to swell”.
quote: Suddenly the tumult ceased, as if by magic, and the doors of the church opened.
quote_source: Alexandre Dumas, The Count of Monte Cristo

definition: Too much pride in your looks or achievements
example: Out of vanity, he refused to wear his glasses in public.
origin: From Old French vanité, from Latin vanitas “emptiness, worthlessness”, from vanus “empty”.
quote: The world had made him extravagant and vain—Extravagance and vanity had made him cold-hearted and selfish.

definition: Physical or mental strength and energy
example: At eighty she still argues with the vigor of a young lawyer.
origin: From Old French vigor, from Latin vigor “liveliness”, from vigere “to be lively, to thrive”.
quote: With unrelaxed nerves, with morning vigor, sail by it, looking another way, tied to the mast like Ulysses.

definition: Severe mental or physical pain
example: The families waited in anguish for news of the rescue.
origin: From Old French anguisse “a choking sensation”, from Latin angustia “narrowness, distress”, from angustus “narrow”.
quote: The anguish of this thought was such that for a moment he almost forgot himself.

definition: The wish to harm or upset other people
example: There was no malice in his joke, only clumsiness.
origin: From Old French malice, from Latin malitia “badness, ill will”, from malus “bad”.
quote: But some enchantment had put both man and woman beyond the reach of malice and unpopularity.

definition: A false reason given to hide the real one
example: He left the meeting early on the pretext of a headache.
origin: From Latin praetextus “outward show”, from praetexere “to weave in front, to disguise”, from prae- “before” and texere “to weave”.
quote: Seizing the first pretext, she got up, and with her light, resolute step went for her album.

definition: Care and concern for someone's comfort or wellbeing
example: The nurse treated every patient with the same quiet solicitude.
origin: From Latin sollicitudo “anxiety”, from sollicitus “agitated, troubled”, from sollus “whole” and citus “set in motion”.
quote: Evening came, and still, with all the patient solicitude of a mother, she watched for his return.
quote_source: Alexandre Dumas, The Count of Monte Cristo

definition: A person's face or its expression
example: His cheerful countenance put the nervous visitors at ease.
origin: From Old French contenance “bearing, behavior”, from Latin continentia “restraint”, from continere “to hold together”.
quote: His countenance, voice, and manner had established him at once in the possession of every virtue.

definition: Friendly and pleasant to be with
example: Our amiable neighbor always stops to chat over the fence.
origin: From Old French amiable, from late Latin amicabilis “friendly”, from Latin amicus “friend”.
quote: The conversation began amiably, but just because it was too amiable, it came to a stop again.

definition: Needing great effort; difficult and tiring
example: The arduous climb to the summit took nearly twelve hours.
origin: From Latin arduus “high, steep, difficult”.
quote: The rest of us must be contented with a fair, but a less arduous, goal.
quote_source: E. M. Forster, A Room with a View

definition: Quick to understand a situation and gain from it
example: An astute observer would have noticed the tension in the room.
origin: From Latin astutus “crafty, clever”, from astus “craft, cunning”.
quote: Thénardier, who was, above all, an astute and well-balanced man, was a scamp of a temperate sort.

definition: Distant and not friendly or involved
example: He remained aloof from the office gossip and ate lunch alone.
origin: From a- “on” and loof, an old form of luff “the windward side of a ship”; a ship kept aloof stayed clear of the shore.
quote: His whole life he had kept aloof from his kind, and he still desired to keep aloof.

definition: Very sad and without hope
example: She grew despondent after her third job application was rejected.
origin: From Latin despondere “to give up, to lose heart”, from de- “away” and spondere “to promise”.
quote: All I see has made me thankful, not despondent.

definition: Causing fear or respect by being large or powerful
example: The champion faces a formidable opponent in tonight's final.
origin: From Latin formidabilis, from formidare “to fear”, from formido “fear, terror”.
quote: The glance of women resembles certain combinations of wheels, which are tranquil in appearance yet formidable.

definition: Proud and looking down on other people
example: The haughty waiter ignored us for nearly half an hour.
origin: From Middle English haut “high, proud”, from Old French haut “high”, from Latin altus.
quote: He had a haughty bearing, a look either steady and impenetrable or insolently piercing and inquisitorial.
quote_source: Alexandre Dumas, The Count of Monte Cristo

definition: Acting quickly without thinking about the results
example: His impetuous decision to quit left the family without income.
origin: From Latin impetuosus, from impetus “attack, rush”, from impetere “to attack”.
quote: Rosamond had that victorious obstinacy which never wastes its energy in impetuous resistance.

definition: So foolish or unreasonable as to be laughable
example: It is ludicrous to expect the work to be done by Friday.
origin: From Latin ludicrus “sportive, done in play”, from ludere “to play”.
quote: We try to find out, but can you imagine anything more ludicrous than one person’s opinion of another person?

definition: Silently bad-tempered and gloomy
example: The sullen teenager answered every question with a shrug.
origin: From Anglo-French solein “alone, solitary”, from Old French sol “alone”, from Latin solus.
quote: A slight wind arose, and the sky looked gray and sullen.

definition: Showing strong and forceful feeling
example: The plan met with vehement opposition from local residents.
origin: From Latin vehemens “violent, eager, impetuous”, of uncertain formation.
quote: She was mortally afraid of being laughed at for surrendering, after her many and vehement declarations of independence.

definition: Full of gentle, sad longing
example: She gave a wistful smile as the train pulled away.
origin: Probably from the obsolete wistly “intently”, with its sense of longing influenced by wishful.
quote: Instead, and after a wistful, searching look, he snuggled in, burrowing his head out of sight between the master’s arm and body.

definition: Rude and not showing proper respect
example: The reporter was told that his question was impertinent.
origin: From late Latin impertinens “not belonging, not to the point”, from in- “not” and pertinere “to pertain”.
quote: I told him of all that had occurred to make my former interference in his affairs absurd and impertinent.

definition: So beautiful or grand as to inspire awe
example: The view from the top of the pass was simply sublime.
origin: From Latin sublimis “uplifted, lofty”, probably from sub “up to” and limen “lintel”.
quote: These sublime and magnificent scenes afforded me the greatest consolation that I was capable of receiving.

definition: Gloomy and depressing, or very bad
example: Ticket sales were dismal during the long, wet summer.
origin: From Anglo-French dis mal, from medieval Latin dies mali “evil days”, the unlucky days of the medieval calendar.
quote: His answer was not cheering to my spirits, for it consisted of two dismal words, ‘With whopping.’

definition: Too ready to believe what you are told
example: Credulous investors lost millions in the scheme.
origin: From Latin credulus “easily believing”, from credere “to believe”.
quote: Oh, in such cases the criminal is often amazingly shallow and credulous.

definition: Quiet and easy to control or teach
example: The horse was docile enough for a child to ride.
origin: From Latin docilis “easily taught”, from docere “to teach”.
quote: Mamma had a little filial lecture afterwards, and was docile as usual.

definition: Expecting obedience in a proud, commanding way
example: With an imperious wave, she sent the waiter away.
origin: From Latin imperiosus “commanding”, from imperium “command, empire”.
quote: The doll is one of the most imperious needs and, at the same time, one of the most charming instincts of feminine childhood.

definition: Persistent in asking, to the point of annoyance
example: He hid in his office to escape the importunate salesmen.
origin: From Latin importunus “unsuitable, troublesome”, originally “having no harbor”, from in- “not” and portus “harbor”.
quote: They were never importunate and yet never listless.
quote_source: Henry James, The Turn of the Screw

definition: Impossible to stop or to persuade
example: The inexorable rise of the sea threatens every village on the coast.
origin: From Latin inexorabilis, from in- “not” and exorare “to prevail upon by pleading”, from orare “to pray, to speak”.
quote: The inexorable facts closed in on him like prison-warders handcuffing a convict.

definition: Deserving or causing public shame
example: The team suffered an ignominious defeat on its own field.
origin: From Latin ignominiosus, from ignominia “loss of good name”, from in- “not” and nomen “name”.
quote: “Brevet,” said the President, “you have undergone an ignominious sentence, and you cannot take an oath.”

definition: Looking or sounding sad in an exaggerated way
example: The lugubrious music made the comedy feel like a funeral.
origin: From Latin lugubris “mournful”, from lugere “to mourn”.
quote: Presently a dog set up a long, lugubrious howl just outside—within ten feet of them.
quote_source: Mark Twain, The Adventures of Tom Sawyer

definition: Having little or no money
example: The impecunious student lived on rice and borrowed books.
origin: From in- “not” and the obsolete pecunious “wealthy”, from Latin pecunia “money”, from pecu “cattle”.

definition: Changing mood or mind quickly and unpredictably
example: Working for such a mercurial director exhausted the whole crew.
origin: From Latin mercurialis “of the god Mercury”, the swift messenger, whose planet was thought to give a lively, changeable nature.
quote: So our mercurial Ladislaw has a queer genealogy!

definition: Very careful about correct behavior and small details
example: She was punctilious about answering every letter within a day.
origin: From Italian puntiglioso, from puntiglio “a fine point”, from Latin punctum “point”.
quote: This quality was continually breaking through his punctilious manner in the shape of restlessness.
quote_source: F. Scott Fitzgerald, The Great Gatsby

definition: Showing steady care, effort and dedication
example: Years of sedulous practice made him a superb pianist.
origin: From Latin sedulus “busy, careful”, probably from se dolo “without deceit”.
quote: Yet there was nothing finicky about their politeness: it had the Public School touch, and, though sedulous, was virile.

definition: Shaking slightly, often from nerves or weakness
example: In a tremulous voice, the witness began to describe the fire.
origin: From Latin tremulus “shaking”, from tremere “to tremble”.
quote: In the garden-scene it had all the tremulous ecstasy that one hears just before dawn when nightingales are singing.
quote_source: Oscar Wilde, The Picture of Dorian Gray

definition: Mocking in a grim or scornful way
example: He greeted the good news with a sardonic little laugh.
origin: From French sardonique, from Greek sardonios, an alteration of sardanios “bitter, scornful” (of laughter), linked in antiquity to a Sardinian plant said to twist the face.
quote: She watched us with a sardonic eye as we stepped from the brougham.
quote_source: Arthur Conan Doyle, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes

definition: Gloomy, serious and slow to smile
example: The saturnine old lawyer rarely spoke at dinner.
origin: From medieval Latin saturninus “of Saturn”; people born under the planet were thought to be cold and gloomy.
quote: A mediæval doctor would have called him saturnine.

definition: Demanding immediate obedience, with no discussion
example: A peremptory knock at the door silenced the whole room.
origin: From Latin peremptorius “final, decisive”, from perimere “to destroy, to take away entirely”.
quote: Now he was peremptory, stern, frowning and for once laying aside all mystification.

definition: Very unhappy and unable to be comforted
example: The disconsolate fans sat in the empty stadium long after the final whistle.
origin: From medieval Latin disconsolatus, from dis- “not” and Latin consolari “to comfort”.
quote: Miserable and disconsolate, he wandered about among the many tents, only to find that one place was as cold as another.
quote_source: Jack London, The Call of the Wild

definition: Causing harm gradually and without being noticed
example: Stress is an insidious problem that builds over many years.
origin: From Latin insidiosus “cunning”, from insidiae “ambush”, from insidere “to sit in wait”.
quote: How insidious he could be, too, I was only to find out several months later and a thousand miles farther.

definition: Having bad habits that cannot be changed
example: My uncle is an incorrigible gambler who never learns.
origin: From Latin incorrigibilis, from in- “not” and corrigere “to correct”.
quote: “Isn’t he incorrigible?” cried Dorian, leaning forward in his chair.
quote_source: Oscar Wilde, The Picture of Dorian Gray

definition: Easily made angry
example: The irascible chef shouted at anyone who entered his kitchen.
origin: From late Latin irascibilis, from Latin irasci “to grow angry”, from ira “anger”.
quote: That hiss, faint as it was, irritated the irascible gentleman, and sealed the culprit’s fate.

definition: Bad-tempered in a childish, sulky way
example: He gave a petulant shrug when asked to wait his turn.
origin: From Latin petulans “impudent, forward”, related to petere “to attack, to seek”.
quote: There was a petulant touch about him—more like a woman.

definition: Good for your health; pleasant and clean
example: They moved to the hills in search of more salubrious air.
origin: From Latin salubris “healthful”, from salus “health”.
quote: The outhouse will do me nicely: it will be more salubrious.
quote_source: James Joyce, A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man

definition: Talking easily, quickly and at length
example: The voluble guide barely paused for breath during the tour.
origin: From Latin volubilis “rolling, flowing”, from volvere “to roll”.
quote: “There is no better,” the voluble Vengeance protested in her shrill notes, “in France.”
quote_source: Charles Dickens, A Tale of Two Cities

definition: Strongly smelling or reminiscent of something
example: The kitchen was redolent of garlic and fresh bread.
origin: From Latin redolens, from redolere “to give off a smell”, from re- (intensive) and olere “to smell”.
quote: Must it not be to that famous elephant, with jewelled tusks, and redolent with myrrh, which was led out of an Indian town to do honor to Alexander the Great?

definition: Giving a good chance of success
example: With interest rates low, it was a propitious moment to buy.
origin: From Latin propitius “favorable, gracious”.
quote: The day was declining, there was not even a cat in the lane, the hour was propitious.

definition: Harmful or unfriendly to something
example: Constant noise is inimical to serious study.
origin: From late Latin inimicalis, from Latin inimicus “enemy”, from in- “not” and amicus “friend”.

definition: Very hard to control, manage or solve
example: Traffic remains the city's most intractable problem.
origin: From Latin intractabilis, from in- “not” and tractare “to handle”.
quote: The spirit which served her was growing intractable: she could neither lay nor control it.

definition: Impossible to calm, satisfy or change
example: She faced an implacable enemy who refused every offer of peace.
origin: From Latin implacabilis, from in- “not” and placare “to calm, to appease”.
quote: The burden is implacable, and remains the same for the few as for the many.

definition: To make a bad situation better
example: New housing would ameliorate conditions for thousands of families.
origin: From French améliorer, from Old French ameillorer, from meillor “better”, from Latin melior.
quote: Philosophy should be an energy; it should have for effort and effect to ameliorate the condition of man.

definition: To make an unpleasant feeling less intense
example: Nothing could assuage her guilt over the missed phone call.
origin: From Old French assouagier, from Latin ad- “to” and suavis “sweet”.
quote: I cannot deny that I grieved for his grief, whatever that was, and would have given much to assuage it.

definition: To catch sight of something far away
example: Through the mist we could just descry the outline of the island.
origin: From Old French descrier “to proclaim, to cry out”; the sense “to catch sight of” comes from a lookout announcing what he saw.
quote: At intervals, truth, that daylight of the human soul, can be descried shining there.

definition: To hide your real feelings or intentions
example: Unable to dissemble, he blushed whenever her name was mentioned.
origin: From Old French dissembler, from Latin dissimulare “to disguise”, reshaped after sembler “to seem”.
quote: Quickly and cleverly she dissembled the astonishment she felt at seeing La Folle.

definition: To express strong disagreement by reasoning with someone
example: I tried to expostulate with him, but he had made up his mind.
origin: From Latin expostulare “to demand urgently”, from ex- “out” and postulare “to demand”.
quote: Sometimes, when the day was very unfavourable, his sisters would expostulate.

definition: To praise something with great enthusiasm
example: Travel writers extol the beaches of the southern coast.
origin: From Latin extollere “to raise up”, from ex- “out, upward” and tollere “to lift”.
quote: It is the humor of many heads to extol the days of their forefathers, and declaim against the wickedness of times present.

definition: To protest or complain forcefully
example: Passengers began to remonstrate with the driver about the delay.
origin: From medieval Latin remonstrare “to show, to point out”, from re- (intensive) and monstrare “to show”.
quote: Henry wished to dissuade me, but seeing me bent on this plan, ceased to remonstrate.

definition: To criticize someone severely for a fault
example: She would upbraid him for every minute he arrived late.
origin: From Old English upbregdan “to bring up as a reproach”, from up and bregdan “to move quickly, to brandish”.
quote: I would rather you had come and upbraided me with vehemence.

definition: To keep changing your mind between choices
example: Voters vacillate between the two candidates from week to week.
origin: From Latin vacillare “to sway, to totter”.
quote: When the relations of a couple are vacillating and neither one thing nor the other, no sort of enterprise can be undertaken.

definition: To drain someone of strength or vitality
example: Long meetings in hot rooms enervate even the keenest staff.
origin: From Latin enervare “to weaken”, literally “to remove the sinews”, from ex- “out” and nervus “sinew”.
quote: What is the nature of the luxury which enervates and destroys nations?

definition: To question whether something is true or honest
example: I do not impugn your motives, only your method.
origin: From Old French impugner, from Latin impugnare “to attack”, from in- “against” and pugnare “to fight”.

definition: Approval or praise, especially formal
example: The plan won the approbation of the entire committee.
origin: From Latin approbatio, from approbare “to approve”, from ad- “to” and probare “to test, to find good”.
quote: A murmur of approbation and satisfaction ran through the crowd.

definition: Shameless and insulting boldness
example: He had the effrontery to ask for a raise after losing the client.
origin: From French effronterie, from effronté “shameless”, from late Latin effrons “barefaced”, from ex- “out” and frons “forehead”.
quote: I wonder—yes I wonder how he has the effrontery to look me in the face, to dare to claim acquaintance with me.
quote_source: E. M. Forster, A Room with a View

definition: Harsh public criticism or disgrace
example: The company faced opprobrium for polluting the river.
origin: From Latin opprobrium “reproach, disgrace”, from ob- “against” and probrum “shameful act”.
quote: I am content to suffer alone while my sufferings shall endure; when I die, I am well satisfied that abhorrence and opprobrium should load my memory.

definition: Bold confidence that seems rude or reckless
example: She had the temerity to correct the professor in front of everyone.
origin: From Latin temeritas “rashness”, from temere “blindly, by chance”.
quote: He stared up disapprovingly over his eye-glasses as Mr. Pontellier entered, wondering who had the temerity to disturb him at that hour of the morning.

definition: A state of physical or mental tiredness
example: A strange lassitude kept him in bed until noon.
origin: From Latin lassitudo, from lassus “weary”.
quote: It was a day of lassitude too, hot and close, with, I am told, a rapidly fluctuating barometer.
quote_source: H. G. Wells, The War of the Worlds

definition: Deliberate betrayal of trust
example: The king never forgave the perfidy of his closest adviser.
origin: From Latin perfidia “faithlessness”, from perfidus “treacherous”, from per- “through, beyond” and fides “faith”.
quote: “Provided I understand your perfidy, sir, and succeed in making you understand that I will be revenged, I shall be reasonable enough,” said Albert furiously.
quote_source: Alexandre Dumas, The Count of Monte Cristo

definition: Complete honesty and strong moral principles
example: Voters trusted the judge for her well-known probity.
origin: From Latin probitas “uprightness”, from probus “good, honest”.
quote: The man of probity sacrifices himself, and out of his very love for this crowd, he combats it.

definition: Morally correct behavior or thinking
example: He was a man of stern rectitude who never told a lie.
origin: From late Latin rectitudo “straightness”, from Latin rectus “straight, right”.
quote: Even much stronger mortals than Fred Vincy hold half their rectitude in the mind of the being they love best.

definition: A state of inactivity and low energy
example: The afternoon heat left the whole village in a torpor.
origin: From Latin torpor “numbness”, from torpere “to be numb or stiff”.
quote: At the sight of another human being my torpor passed, and I leaned out of the window eagerly.
quote_source: H. G. Wells, The War of the Worlds

definition: Wicked or shameful character or behavior
example: The court found him guilty of an act of moral turpitude.
origin: From Latin turpitudo “baseness”, from turpis “ugly, shameful”.
quote: As for the moral turpitude that man unveiled to me, even with tears of penitence, I can not, even in memory, dwell on it without a start of horror.
quote_source: Robert Louis Stevenson, The Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde

definition: A state of extreme poverty
example: The once-famous painter died in penury in a rented room.
origin: From Latin penuria “want, scarcity”.
quote: It contained but two rooms, and these exhibited all the squalidness of the most miserable penury.

definition: A sudden, violent burst of emotion or activity
example: The joke sent the whole class into a paroxysm of laughter.
origin: From Greek paroxysmos “irritation, a severe fit”, from paroxynein “to provoke, to sharpen”, from para- “beyond” and oxys “sharp”.
quote: The child, hearing its mother’s voice, broke out into a paroxysm of sobbing.

definition: Speed of movement or action
example: The rumor spread through the village with remarkable celerity.
origin: From Latin celeritas, from celer “swift”.
quote: Van Helsing returned with extraordinary celerity, bearing with him a surgical case.

definition: A person who dislikes people and avoids them
example: The old misanthrope lived alone and spoke to no one.
origin: From Greek misanthropos, from misein “to hate” and anthropos “human being”.
quote: He had absolutely nothing to do, almost died of ennui, and became a confirmed misanthrope.
quote_source: Oscar Wilde, The Picture of Dorian Gray

definition: A sign that something is about to happen
example: The first swallow is a harbinger of spring.
origin: From Old French herbergere “one who provides lodging”, from herberge “lodging”, of Germanic origin; a harbinger once went ahead of an army to arrange shelter.
